sources.news_title: No Kings rallies across US urge voters to cast ballots early ahead of midterms - WSVN 7News | Miami News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
Rallies organized by the No Kings network opposed to President Donald Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections.
The hundreds of planned events were billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years’ worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump’s presidency.
A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!” were among the many signs held aloft.
At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
“The Constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?” he said.
“You don’t see Superman giving up his power,” Bond continued. “You don’t see Black Panther giving up his power. You don’t see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a super hero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote.”
Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election.
His administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
On Friday the Justice Department warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
Earlier that day Democratic Sens. Alex Padilla of California, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Dick Durbin of Illinois wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

sources.news_title: Michigan No Kings rallies blend anti-Trump protests with calls to vote early
sources.text:
Michigan No Kings rallies blend anti-Trump protests with calls to vote early
Attendees gathered on the West Lawn of the Michigan State Capitol for the No Kings rally in Lansing on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Thousands of demonstrators gathered at No Kings rallies across Michigan on Saturday as organizers hoped to turn the movement’s opposition to President Donald Trump into increased voter turnout in November’s midterm elections.
With early in-person voting set to begin statewide next weekend, rallies in Lansing, Ferndale and Grand Rapids were among dozens across the state that combined criticism of the Trump administration with calls for voters to make a plan to cast their ballots and help protect the election process.
Lansing’s No Kings protest on the West Lawn of the Michigan State Capitol was heavily focused on encouraging attendees to vote — especially using early voting methods, including absentee ballots and early in-person voting, the latter of which begins on Oct. 24 in Michigan.
Much like at past No Kings events, many signs in the crowd of a few hundred attendees were critical or mocking of President Donald Trump and his policies, including those around immigration enforcement. Disapproval of the current federal administration was an overarching theme among attendees.
Anne Paquet Howard, 78, a Lansing resident, reminisced on her time campaigning for Robert F. Kennedy as a student at Michigan State University in the 1960s. She said it taught her “the importance of one person, one vote.”
“I was a part of the Great Society, and I think that’s one of the eras where America was really working more towards a perfect union. And it saddens my heart to see what’s developed since then, so I’ll be here and thankfully I’m still healthy,” she said. “The big message is get out to vote, everyone, please, it still works.”
“Make your plans to vote early and be the election protectors we know you can be,” Alyson Grigsby, an organizer with Voters Not Politicians, told the crowd.
Throughout the rally, organizers posed hypotheticals about situations that could arise on Election Day, such an ICE presence at a polling location, and discussed how they might respond — alerting relevant local leaders, including the precinct captains and local clerks, and reporting incidents to election protection organizations.
Speakers heavily encouraged anyone with concerns on or leading up to Election Day to make use of a nonpartisan voter hotline, but also encouraged voters to verify information that they may see on social media about elections with trusted sources like the ACLU or election officers.
“It’s important to leave today not only knowing you have a plan to vote early, but also have a plan to keep our elections and our communities safe, on Election Day and the days afterwards,” Grigsby said.
The focus on early voting was clear from organizers ahead of Saturday’s event, and the rally itself included opportunities for attendees to sign up to be poll watchers or poll challengers on Election Day.
Also present at Lansing’s rally were booths for various political organizations, including the Ingham County Democratic Party and those in favor of Michigan’s Proposition 2, the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot measure to limit campaign spending by utility companies and government contractors.
In Ferndale, one of southeast Michigan’s larger rallies drew several hundred demonstrators to the intersection of 9 Mile Road and Woodward Avenue, with a mix of signs both encouraging voters to cast their ballots and simultaneously excoriating the actions of the Trump administration.
Even though this iteration of No Kings activity was supposed to be about encouraging people to vote, the signs that dozens of demonstrators carried and waved at traffic lambasted the Trump administration, ICE, and the president’s stress-testing the limits of executive power.
@michiganadvance Tyler Scott – aka @T Moscotto – breaks down the No Kings rally in Ferndale. @No kings #nokings ♬ original sound – Michigan Advance 
The pro-voting activism was happening where volunteers with the anti-authoritarian activist network Indivisible and their partners asked those attending the rally about their plans to vote, and whether they felt knowledgeable about the ballot proposals Michiganders statewide will be voting on in November, along with the candidates for elected office.
“For my granddaughters I feel like I need to stand up for their future, all my grandkids’ future, and especially our girls, their human rights,” Julie Bloss of St. Clair Shores, Michigan said when asked why she was attending the Ferndale gathering.
Stephen Machlay of Detroit was more blunt in his rationale for attending the rally.
“I’m tired of fascism in America. Our economy is in shambles. The tariffs are a disaster. He’s making enemies of all our allies and friends with all our enemies,” Machlay said, referring to Trump.
Traffic honked, mostly in friendly affirmation of the anti-Trump administration signs. There was one noticeable moment of minor counter-protesting, when a Trump supporter yelled “four more years” and shook his fist at a person in a full-body furry suit who held a sign reading “melt that ICE.”
Meanwhile, in West Michigan, No Kings drew people to Rosa Parks Circle in downtown Grand Rapids, which was filled with hundreds of demonstrators Saturday morning as part of the nationwide day of action, officially dubbed “No Kings: Vote Early.”
The demonstration — which focused on impacting polls on a local scale — featured speakers from Indivisible Kent County, Unite and Resist Grand Rapids and UCC Power Fund, as well as a live performance by Asamu Johnson and the Associates of the Blues.
Jim Hollebeek, who attended Saturday’s demonstration, used to teach American history. He said he’s disappointed by the direction the nation is going.
“This is not the country that I taught about, and that saddens me a lot,” he said. “I think it’s time people got together and took that country back to where it was and where it ought to be.”
Hollebeek and his daughter Kim Dewey live in Grand Rapids, and they’ve attended all four downtown No Kings demonstrations together.
The two said Saturday’s event wasn’t as well-advertised as previous protests, but they hope it will still impact the midterm elections.
“That’d be awesome if everyone would get out and make their voices heard, because that’s their right,” Dewey said. “I’m hopeful that we take over both the House and the Senate.”

sources.news_title: "No Kings" anti-Trump movement organizes thousands of rallies to boost early voting in midterms
sources.text:
"No Kings" anti-Trump movement organizes thousands of rallies to boost early voting in midterms
Washington DC - As Americans begin casting their ballots in the midterm elections, the prominent "No Kings" anti-Trump movement is organizing thousands of rallies Saturday to get voters fired up.
"No Kings" has more than 3,000 events planned across the US for its fourth iteration since President Donald Trump returned to office, this time with a special twist for the November 3 vote.
Dubbed "No Kings: Vote Early," the events on Saturday aim to get out the vote rather than protest the actions of Trump and his Republican administration.
"It's a day of nonpartisan voter participation: we are bringing our community together to make a plan to vote early and ensuring every eligible voter understands their options for how to vote and has the opportunity to make their voice heard," organizers said in a statement.
Saturday's itinerary varies widely depending on the location, from a music festival in Los Angeles and a march to the Supreme Court in Washington, to family-friendly workshops in Chicago and election observer training in Atlanta.
"No Kings: Early Vote will be thousands of joyful celebrations of our right to vote across the country," said Deirdre Schifeling, the chief political and advocacy officer of the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the partner organizations behind Saturday's events.
"No Kings" rallies aim at "reclaiming voting"
Although Tuesday, November 3 is election day, most areas of the US allow voters to cast their ballots ahead of time, sometimes weeks in advance.
Alma Couverthie, who oversees grassroots organizing efforts for democracy watchdog organization Common Cause, said the point of the upcoming "No Kings" rallies is "reclaiming voting for what it truly is: an act of power, an act of service, and an act of joy."
"This Saturday, October 17, will be a celebration of our collective power. Walk together to the polls. Organize rides. Bring your neighbors, friends, and family," she urged participants.
Trump has openly criticized the practice of mail-in voting, and opponents have expressed concern that the administration will attempt to undermine the results – especially if Republicans end up losing, as opinion polls show is quite likely.
By advocating for voting early, the "No Kings" organizers hope to cut off the potential for any malfeasance once election day rolls around.
"The best way to prevent any funny business from this administration after election day is to make sure that our turnout is massive, so clear and so overwhelming that our victory for democracy is impossible to question," Couverthie said.
Cover photo: GIORGIO VIERA / AFP

sources.news_title: ‘Vote early’: No Kings rallies focus on voter turnout in midterm elections
sources.text:
What to know
- The No Kings coalition that has driven millions of people to the streets across the country during President Donald Trump’s second term returned today with a unique focus: getting Americans to vote in the midterm elections just 17 days away. The collective event dubbed “No Kings: Vote Early,” drew tens of thousands of people at rallies in some 3,000 cities across the United States with a focus on “putting power back in the hands of the people,” according to organizers.
- At one point today, No Kings organizers accused Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, of taking its Instagram account down for over an hour as rallies reached their peak. Meta did not immediately comment.
- Protestors turned out in Trump’s backyards — in the nation’s capital and on the streets near Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, where the president is spending the weekend. He left for several hours today to headline a rally in Kentucky for Republican candidates. The Blue Grass State is one of many areas where Republicans find themselves playing defense in a volatile midterm election landscape.
- Previous No Kings rallies were larger, drawing millions of people repudiating Trump’s policies and actions, including his war against Iran, the soaring cost of living and aggressive immigration crackdowns in cities like Minneapolis, where Renee Good and Alex Pretti were killed by federal officers.

sources.news_title: No Kings turns its focus to voting this weekend. Here's what we know
sources.text:
No Kings, the coalition known for organizing anti-Trump protests, is trying a different democratic tactic: increasing voter turnout.
On Saturday, grassroot groups across the country will hold over 3,000 "No Kings: Vote Early" marches and other events. Organizers say these events are a nonpartisan effort to promote early voting in the midterm elections, and will involve helping people check their voter registration, make a plan to cast their ballot and understand their voting rights.
The voting push effort marks a pivot for the No Kings coalition, which comprises hundreds of partner organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union and Black Voters Matter.
No Kings has previously held three days of nationwide protests since the start of Trump's second term because organizers say Trump's actions in office are more akin to those of a monarch than a democratically elected head of state. Trump has previously rejected the idea that he is behaving like a monarch.
"The first three No Kings were designed to send a message," says Ezra Levin, the co-founder of Indivisible — one of the major organizations within the No Kings network. "We're done sending a message."
Now, he says, they want people to vote.
There are two main goals for the event, says Levin, the first is to help facilitate what he hopes will be the largest number of midterm early voting numbers in the country's history.
The second goal is No Kings groups getting volunteers trained as poll watchers, an endeavor Levin says is in response to efforts by the Trump administration that he views as threats to election integrity. Levin points to the failed SAVE America Act that would have required voters to show a document proving their U.S. citizenship, such as a passport or a birth certificate, when registering to vote. He also raises concerns that federal immigration officers will be sent to the polls, and President Trump's attempted restrictions on voting by mail.
What do organizers expect nationwide?
Saturday's events vary widely across the country, from block parties to cookouts to rallies. In Golden, Colo., a "Paws to the Polls" event invites people to bring their dogs on a march. Organizers in Everett, Wash., planned a "concert for democracy," featuring an environmental troubadour.
All events will share similar restrictions, Levin says, including a rule against political endorsements and inviting current candidates to speak.
Superhero capes and masks will be a staple of Cammy Dunford's event in Frisco, Texas. Dunford, a co-leader of Indivisible Frisco, plans to hold a "voting is your superpower" gathering. She will be wearing a red and blue cape (to embrace the political spectrum of voters) and will give away other superhero capes and masks.
"I don't care if you're an independent, first-time voter, Democrat, Republican," Dunford says, "if you are eligible to vote, you need to get out there and vote. Because without everybody voting, we don't have a democracy."
Early voting in Texas does not start until Oct. 19, but Dunford and a group of her neighbors put together 500 mini goodie bags to hand out — filled with QR codes linking to voting information and voting resources. They will also wave bright signs with superhero-shaped images urging people in passing cars to vote.
Dunford says that her group has two people already trained as poll monitors and is hoping to recruit more on Saturday. She says poll monitors are trained by Common Cause, a government watchdog group that equips them to answer questions from voters. They have T-shirts that identify them at the polls, she says, so voters can find them and ask questions.
At a Wyandotte, Mich., event, Christy McGillivray, the executive director of Voters Not Politicians, a nonpartisan advocacy organization, is scheduled to speak to a No Kings crowd about the history of fighting for democracy in the U.S. She says the organization of grassroots events across the country is inspiring.
"It makes people feel like they're a part of something bigger than themselves," she says. "And that's what democracy is. Democracy is about working with each other and for each other."

sources.news_title: Nationwide No Kings protests push for historic early voting results
Oct. 17 No Kings standouts promoting early voting
sources.text:
No Kings activists are staging coordinated events across the region and country this Saturday to promote early voting for next month’s elections.
According to a press release more than 3,000 No Kings events are planned nationwide on Oct. 17. Local standouts organized by Indivisible First Middlesex and Indivisible Fitchburg MA include several stops that are part of the Vote Early Express effort, including two locations in Fitchburg — from 10 to 11:30 a.m. at the Route 2/Route 31 overpass and also from 10 to 11:30 a.m. at the Electric Avenue/South Street intersection.
Additional events are being held in Lowell, Ashby, Groton, Lunenburg, Pepperell and Townsend, and activists at each location will display Burma Shave style signs promoting early voting.
“This round of No Kings events will stress visibility over numbers,” said Michael Immerso of Indivisible First Middlesex. “What matters now is getting people to the polls. Voting early is important because it increases voter turnout. We will be bringing that message directly to the electorate.”
The times and locations for the local No Kings standouts stops in the North Central Mass area as follows”
• Fitchburg: 10 to 11:30 a.m. at the Route 2/Route 31 overpass and also from .
• Fitchburg: 10 to 11:30 a.m. at the Electric Avenue/South Street intersection
• Lowell: Noon to 2 p.m. at Jack Kerouac Park
• Chelmsford: 10 to 11:30 a.m. at Chelmsford Town Common
• Billerica: 11:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. at Billerica Town Hall
• Ashby: 1:30 to 2:30 p.m. outside the library
• Groton: 9 to 10 a.m. at the intersection of Routes 119 and 225
• Lunenburg: 3 to 4 p.m. at the corner of Main Street and Massachusetts Avenue
• Pepperell: 10:30 to 11:30 a.m. at the town rotary
• Townsend: Noon to 1 p.m. on the town common on Route 119
• Littleton: 10 a.m. to noon at Littleton Common
To find a protest near you visit indivisible.org, which has this message on its website:
“Trump is trying to sabotage the midterms. On October 17, millions will rise up to defend our right to vote, exercise that right through the largest early vote mobilization in history and tap into efforts to protect the results.”
Indivisible Fitchburg will also be at the two standouts in the city. Cindy Jackson, one of the group organizers, relayed that while they are “not in partnership with any other Indivisibles per se, we often coordinate with area Indivisibles to be sure our events don’t overlap or interrupt other events.”
She went on to say it is important to the Indivisible Fitchburg members to once again participate in the No Kings protests, this one is the fourth iteration since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025 for his second term.
“With demonstrations taking place here and around the country on Saturday, we are letting our neighbors know that early voting has begun and is so important,” Jackson conveyed. “Our goal is to turn out as many early voters as possible. When we vote, we win.”

Thousands of 'No Kings' protests held nationwide as early voting begins
sources.text:
Thousands of ‘No Kings’ protests held nationwide as early voting begins
TheHill.com reported on Oct. 17 that thousands of “No Kings” protests were held across the country on Oct. 17 for a nationwide day of action amid the start of early voting in many states.
The Hill’s story said previous nationwide protest days led by the No Kings Coalition have been aimed at denouncing President Trump and his administration’s policies.
Source: TheHill.com Just In
